entities.name: Simone Pasqua
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Simone Pasqua (1492–1565) was an influential Italian Roman Catholic cardinal and bishop whose career unfolded during the tumultuous intellectual and religious landscape of the High Renaissance and the early Counter-Reformation. Born in Taggia, Liguria, Pasqua rose through the ecclesiastical ranks, becoming a key figure in the Church's administrative structure and a participant in the pivotal Council of Trent. His trajectory reflects the opportunities and challenges faced by ambitious churchmen navigating a period of profound theological debate, political maneuvering, and artistic flourishing across the Italian peninsula.

Pasqua's ascent began with his legal studies, culminating in a doctorate in utroque iure (canon and civil law), which positioned him for administrative roles within the Church. He served as an auditor of the Sacred Roman Rota, a significant ecclesiastical court, and was a referendary of the Apostolic Signatura, demonstrating his deep involvement in papal jurisprudence. His ecclesiastical career saw him appointed Bishop of Luni e Sarzana in Italy in 1561, a position he held until his elevation to cardinal by Pope Pius IV in 1565. As cardinal, he was first assigned the titulus of Santa Sabina, quickly followed by San Pancrazio, marking his entry into the College of Cardinals.

His participation in the final sessions of the Council of Trent (1545–1563) was a defining aspect of his career, placing him at the heart of the Catholic Church's efforts to reform itself and respond to the Protestant Reformation. Although his cardinalate was brief, lasting only a few months before his death in September 1565, his presence on the Council and his legal expertise contributed to the formulation of decrees that would shape Catholic doctrine and practice for centuries. Pasqua's legacy lies in his contribution to the institutional strengthening of the Church during a critical period of renewal.
